Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:5: The Shema — you already know that it is the unification of the Omnipresent, which is the root of all the commandments; it also has 248 words, for through its recitation the 248 limbs of the soul are set right; and our Sages, of blessed memory, also said (Menachot 39b), whoever recites the Shema twice each day, it is as though he had fulfilled the entire Torah, as it is said (Joshua 1:8), "and you shall meditate on it day and night":
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:6: Prayer — our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 32b), it is among the things that stand at the very height of the world, and as you know, it is greater than all the sacrifices, as it is said (Isaiah 1:11), "why do I need your many sacrifices," and it is written, "even though you multiply prayer" — implying it is greater than they are. And just as sacrifices atone, prayer likewise atones for a person's sins. And in Sefer HaZohar, Parashat Vayakhel (201b): prayer is more precious than all forms of worship and than all sacrifices [prayer is more honored than all forms of divine service and than all sacrifices]:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:7: Causing merit to the guilty (guiding sinners back to merit) — our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Eliyahu Rabbah, end of ch. 8), why did Elkanah merit to raise up Samuel, who is weighed as equal to Moses and Aaron? Because he would go up for the pilgrimage festival and bring many other people up together with him, causing them merit; and likewise his son Samuel followed his practice, as it is written (I Samuel 7:16), "and he went around to Beit El and Gilgal... and he judged Israel," "and his return was to Ramah, for there was his house." And Abraham merited all his virtues only on account of (Genesis 12:5), "and the souls that they had made in Charan" [i.e., the souls he had converted], and it is written (ibid. 18:19), "for I have known him, that he will command..." "and they shall keep the way of the Lord..." And all the leaders of the generations merit or are punished only for this reason:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:8: And in Sefer HaZohar, the beginning of Parashat Terumah (128b), it enlarges upon praising this commandment, and says: the meritorious one must pursue the guilty and acquire him for a complete reward, and so on, and this is the praise by which the glory of the Holy One, blessed be He, is elevated more than by any other praise, and this ascent is greater than everything, and so on; and concerning this it is written of Aaron (Malachi 2), "and turned many away from iniquity," and it is written, "My covenant of life and peace was with him," and so on, and he ascended in three ascents, in a way no other person ascends, and concerning this person it is written, "My covenant of life and peace was with him," and he merits to see children born to his children, and he merits in this world and merits the World to Come, and enters through thirteen gates, and no one can prevent him, and of him it is written (Psalms 112:2), "his descendants shall be mighty in the land," "wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever, light dawns in the darkness for the upright." Then the Holy King blesses the image of that person with all the blessings He blessed Abraham with, when he made souls for the guilty, and so on; and he enters into seventy hidden worlds that no other person merits. And if people knew how much benefit and merit is brought about for the righteous and for those who merit through them, they would follow after them and pursue them as one pursues life, and so on:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:9: <small>[Translation — In Sefer HaZohar, the beginning of Parashat Terumah: the meritorious one must pursue people who are liable and acquire them for a complete reward, and this is the praise through which the glory of the Holy One, blessed be He, is elevated more than by any other praise, and this ascent is more than everything. And of this it is written of Aaron, "and turned many away from iniquity." And it is written, "My covenant of life and peace was with him" — and that person is elevated in three ascents, in a manner no other person is elevated. And of this person it is written, "My covenant of life and peace was with him," and he merits to see children born to his children, and merits in this world and merits the World to Come, and ascends through thirteen gates, and no one can prevent his hand, and of him it is written, "his descendants shall be mighty in the land — wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever; light dawns in the darkness for the upright." Then the holy King blesses the image of that person with all the blessings He blessed Abraham with, when he made souls for those who were liable, and he ascends to seventy hidden worlds that no other person has merited. And had people known how much benefit and merit is drawn to the righteous and to those who merit through them, they would go after them and pursue them like one who pursues life.]</small>:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:10: Conducting business faithfully — this was already explained (in Gate Five) regarding the matter of deceit; see there. You also know that a person's judgment after his passing begins with, "did you conduct your business faithfully" (Shabbat 31a):
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:11: Charity is explained in Isaiah (58:7), "is it not to share your bread with the hungry..." "then you shall call and the Lord shall answer, you shall cry and He shall say, here I am," and it is written (Deuteronomy 15:10), "for because of this thing the Lord your God shall bless you," and it is written (Proverbs 21:14), "a gift in secret subdues anger," (Proverbs 17) "and charity delivers from death," and it is written (Psalms 112:3, 9), "and his righteousness endures forever." And no transgression extinguishes it, as it does other commandments, and it brings life to a person, as in the incident of Binyamin HaTzaddik mentioned by our Sages, of blessed memory (Bava Batra 11a):
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:12: Honoring the Sabbath — it is known that the Sabbath is weighed as equal to the entire Torah, as was explained at the beginning of this gate concerning the Sabbath; see there. And it is written (Isaiah 58:13), "if you turn back your foot from the Sabbath..." "and call the Sabbath a delight..." "then I will make you ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed you with the heritage of your father Jacob." And there is an incident (Shabbat 118b) about Yosef Mokir Shabbat, who merited to acquire all the tremendous wealth of that gentile. And there is an incident (ibid.) about a certain man who ate at a table of gold requiring sixteen men to carry, on which were all kinds of delicacies created since the six days of Creation; I said to him, my son, how did you merit all this wealth? He answered, I was a butcher, and whenever I found a fine animal I would say, "this is for the Sabbath," and so on; and our Sages, of blessed memory, said, by what merit do the wealthy of outside the Land [of Israel] merit their wealth? Because they honor the Sabbath:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:13: Circumcising one's son — if [the reward for] causing merit to the guilty is beyond measure, as we explained, how much more so bringing one's own son beneath the wings of the Shechinah, which takes precedence over doing this for others:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:14: Acts of loving-kindness, visiting the sick, bringing peace, and welcoming guests — these are among the things whose fruit a person enjoys in this world while the principal remains for him in the World to Come; and of one who occupies himself with Torah and with acts of loving-kindness, the Holy One, blessed be He, says, I credit it to him as though he had redeemed Me and My children from among the nations; and this was the trait of Abraham, as it is written (Micah 7:20), "You shall give truth to Jacob, kindness to Abraham," and it is written (Proverbs 21:21), "whoever pursues righteousness and kindness shall find life, righteousness, and honor,"
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:15: and Abaye, who came from the house of Eli (Rosh Hashanah 18a), because he occupied himself with acts of loving-kindness, had twenty years added to his life, more than his teacher Rabbah bar Nachmani; and they save one from the judgment of Gehinnom and from chibut hakever (the beating of the grave), as mentioned above in Gate Two:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:16: Setting fixed times for Torah study was explained in Gate Five regarding mockery, and it is known that Torah study is weighed as equal to all the commandments, and that a person's judgment begins with, "did you set fixed times for Torah," as it is said (Proverbs 17:14), "the beginning of strife is like the letting out of water":
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:17: And these are the good customs:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:18: The Shema recited upon one's bed — you know what our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Zohar III, 211a), whoever recites the Shema upon his bed kills many myriads of harmful spirits present at night, and especially so when the soul ascends on high, as it is written (Psalms 149:5), "let the pious exult in glory, let them sing for joy upon their beds — the exaltation of God is in their throats":
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 7:19: Rising after midnight — apart from its being among [the practices of] those who mourn for Zion and Jerusalem, of whom it is said (Isaiah 66), "rejoice with her, all who mourn for her" — for the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself mourns and roars like a lion at that very hour. Also, regarding occupying oneself then with Torah, our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:7), there is no song of Torah except at night; and our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Avodah Zarah 3b), whoever occupies himself with Torah at night, a thread of kindness is drawn over him by day; and our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Tamid 32b), whoever occupies himself with Torah at night, the Shechinah is opposite him; and it is written (Lamentations 2:19), "arise, cry out in the night"; and King David, peace be upon him, merited to live and endure in this world and in the World to Come only for this practice, as it is written (Psalms 119:62), "at midnight I rise to give thanks to You." And throughout the whole Sefer HaZohar, the praises of this commandment are explained without end; it also causes the Holy Spirit to rest upon a person, as mentioned there in Parashat Shemot (18b):
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:1-3: Called the Gate of Repentance, and is divided into three parts.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:4: The most grave among all of them are the positive commandments regarding the Paschal offering and circumcising oneself, whose neglect carries karet. More severe than these, positive commandments whose neglect carries both a negative prohibition and karet, such as afflicting oneself [fasting] and resting from labor on Yom Kippur. Higher than this, resting from labor on the Sabbath, whose neglect carries both a negative prohibition and stoning. Higher than this, being fruitful and multiplying, for even if he possesses Torah and mitzvot like Hezekiah, he will die in this world and not live in the World to Come [if he neglects it]; and likewise the positive commandment of donning tefillin — if one is "one whose head has never worn tefillin" at all, he does not arise in the resurrection of the dead, and is called among the transgressors of Israel in body. Greater than all of these is one who breaks the covenant [refuses circumcision] out of spite:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:5: And the positive commandment to know that there is a God — one who denies this fundamental principle has no share in the World to Come:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:6: There are also commandments whose fruit one enjoys in this world while the principal remains for him in the World to Come: honoring father and mother; acts of loving-kindness with one's body and one's money, for the poor and for the rich; bringing joy to a bride and groom; visiting the sick; burying the dead; comforting mourners; clothing the naked; welcoming guests; attentiveness in prayer with intention; bringing peace between one person and another — and how much more so between oneself and one's own fellow, and included in this is judging one's fellow favorably; and Torah study, which is equal to all of them, and included in this is rising early for the synagogue and raising one's children to Torah study:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:7: The second part: On the punishment for forbidden character traits and for negative commandments:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:8: The two most grave bad character traits are: anger, which is weighed as equal to idolatry, in which he tears his own soul in his anger, and it is uprooted from there and departs, and is replaced by another, evil soul;
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:9: higher than it is pride and haughtiness of spirit, which is weighed as equal to idolatry, to an Asherah tree, to an abomination, to denying the fundamental principle, and it is as though he had committed all forbidden sexual relations, and even his dust is not stirred at the resurrection of the dead. And indeed, regarding the punishment for negative commandments, some of them carry the prohibition of a negative commandment for which there is no lashing, such as a prohibition without an action, or one that is subsumed into a positive commandment. Higher than these are those for which one receives lashing:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:10: These two categories, as well as the neglect of every positive commandment other than the grave ones mentioned above, are all called light transgressions; and all the grave positive commandments mentioned above, as well as every negative commandment other than these two categories mentioned, are all called grave transgressions, and there are many gradations among them, and these are they: all those liable to karet and death at the hand of Heaven, and death by the court.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:11: "You shall not take the Name of the Lord your God in vain" — although it carries no karet, in one respect it is more severe than all the others, for punishment comes upon him and upon his family and upon the entire world, even upon those who had no power to protest.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:12: Regarding the matter of the desecration of the Name (Yoma 86a): and to what extent does the desecration of the Name reach? Rav said, such as myself — if I take meat and do not pay for it immediately. Rabbi Yochanan said, such as myself — if I walk four cubits without Torah or tefillin, due to weakness, yet the onlooker does not know it was due to weakness and learns from me to neglect Torah and tefillin. Rabbi Yannai says, whenever one's associates are ashamed of him because of the bad reputation that has gone out about him. Abaye said, as it was taught: "and you shall love the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 6:5) — that Heaven's Name become beloved through you, so that people say of him: he reads and reviews, and so on, and conducts his business dealings faithfully and speaks gently with people; but if his business dealings are not conducted faithfully, Heaven's Name is desecrated through him:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:13: And all of these, if he did not repent and died, are judged in Gehinnom, and in the end they chirp their way up from there and ascend, and they have a remedy, and the resurrection of the dead, and the World to Come:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:14: Higher than this are the transgressors of Israel in body: "one whose head has never worn tefillin" at all, who was lazy about donning them though he was able to — for if it was out of spite, he is called a heretic or at least an apostate — and if he died without repenting, he is judged in Gehinnom for twelve months, and afterward his body is consumed and his soul is burned and becomes ash beneath the soles of the feet of the righteous in the World to Come:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:15: Higher than this are those who have no share whatsoever in the World to Come, and Gehinnom itself is consumed while they are not consumed, even though they possess Torah learning and good deeds and did not repent and died, like Doeg the Edomite, the mightiest of the shepherds. And these are they: the heretics, and their students, who twist words of Torah into heresy; and likewise one who apostatizes to idolatry alone, even though he acknowledges all the other commandments and has become habituated in constant idol worship,
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:16: and apostates, and likewise one who apostatizes regarding any one transgression among the other transgressions out of spite, even for the sake of mere appetite; and one who casts off the yoke [of the commandments], meaning one who denies the fundamental principle and says there is no God; and likewise one who says, there is Torah from Heaven, but I do not accept it — meaning, I do not fulfill it; and one who says the Torah is not from Heaven, even regarding a single verse or a single fine point of an extra or missing letter, or a single a fortiori inference, or a single verbal analogy — and some say even regarding the Oral Torah or the words of the Sages; and one who says the resurrection of the dead is not from the Torah — meaning that its concept is not alluded to in the Torah, even though he believes in the Torah and that there is a resurrection of the dead; and one who distorts the meaning of the Torah improperly, such as Menasseh, who expounded degrading legends, [asking] what need did Moses have to write in the Torah "and Lotan's sister was Timna," and the like; and likewise one who transgresses the words of Torah with a high hand, publicly, like Jehoiakim; and one who breaks the covenant of his flesh, refusing to circumcise himself out of spite; and likewise one who pulls his foreskin forward to appear uncircumcised; and one who sins and also causes the multitude to sin, like Jeroboam, even in a light transgression; and the apikoros (heretic/scoffer), who is one who disgraces a Torah scholar in his presence; and likewise a student who sits before his teacher and says, this thing is forbidden or permitted, casually, and not by way of a question; and likewise one who mocks his teacher when he expounds some matter of exaggeration and does not believe his words; and likewise one who disgraces a Torah scholar not in his presence, such as those who say disparagingly, "these rabbis," or those who say, what use are the rabbis to us — for themselves they call [something forbidden] and for themselves they permit [it]; or those who say, what use are the rabbis to us — have they ever forbidden us the raven or permitted us the dove? Or a student who calls his teacher by his own name and does not say "my master and my teacher"; and likewise one who disgraces his fellow in the presence of a Torah scholar; and informers, whether one who hands a Jew over to a gentile to be beaten, or hands over his money; and a leader who casts excessive dread upon the community in order to be haughty and not for the sake of Heaven; and one who disgraces the festivals by doing work on the intermediate days of a festival in a spirit of contempt, not believing in this prohibition and not for his own benefit; and one who shames his fellow publicly to his face; and one who glorifies himself through another's shame — and it seems to me that this too applies [only] when done to his face; and one who reads external books, such as Sefer Ben Sira and the books of Ben La'anah, which are frivolous matters that draw a person's heart after them, and through this he is kept from words of Torah, and likewise the books of the heretics — but the books of Homer and all their other kinds of books are regarded merely as reading a letter, as they said in the Yerushalmi (Sanhedrin ch. 10, halachah 1); and one who whispers over a wound and recites a verse and spits — and this is not only regarding a verse in which there is mention of illness and healing and the Name of Heaven, but even such as "And the Lord spoke to Moses," and so on; and one who utters the Name of God outside [the Temple] by its letters — and they explained in the Yerushalmi there that this means he does not refer to it by its appellation, as it is written, "this is My name and this is My remembrance" — but in our own Talmud (Avodah Zarah 18) [this applies] specifically in a gathering of people; and one who treats the word of God with contempt, meaning one who mentions words of Torah in a filthy place; and likewise one who reads the Written Torah and does not pay attention to the Mishnah, which is its interpretation; and likewise one who learns Torah and does not teach it — except regarding the secrets of the Torah, of which it is written (Proverbs 27:26), "lambs for your clothing" — only for the pious of the generation who are fit for it; and likewise one who is able to occupy himself with Torah but does not, occupying himself instead with commerce and worldly affairs; and the gossip-monger, who carries reports from one to another, even if they are not disparaging words and even if they are true, as with Doeg regarding David; and one who speaks evil speech, telling of his fellow's disgrace even though it is true; and one who spreads a bad name about his fellow, telling of his disgrace when it is not true — and these three, the gossip-monger, the speaker of evil speech, and the spreader of a bad name, are as though they had denied the fundamental principle, and are grave, weighed as equal to the three most grave transgressions in the whole Torah, which are idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed; one who lends with interest and does not repay does not arise in the resurrection of the dead; and one who desecrates the Sabbath is judged in Gehinnom for all generations; and one who deliberately neglects being fruitful and multiplying and dies without children dies subject to karet in this world and shall not live in the World to Come:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:17: Three go down to Gehinnom and never come up: one who has relations with a married woman, and one who gives his fellow a demeaning nickname, even though the person has become accustomed to it and is not ashamed, so long as the intent is to humiliate him — yet both of these have a share in the World to Come; only one who actually shames another publicly to his face has no share in the World to Come. Four things a person enjoys the fruits of in this world while the principal remains for him in the World to Come: idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, bloodshed, and evil speech, which is weighed as equal to all three of them, and moreover has no share in the World to Come.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:18: Greater than all transgressions is one who emits his own seed in vain, for he spills the blood of his own seed's offspring until the end of the world, and moreover, all other transgressions can be rectified through repentance, but this one has no [full] repentance, as mentioned in Sefer HaZohar, Parashat Vayechi (219b) — and some have the reading, "unless through greater and constant strength [of repentance]":
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:19: Transgressions between man and his fellow are lighter than all transgressions between man and the Omnipresent, and yet, in another respect, are more grave than all of them, for they have no remedy at all until he appeases his fellow and his fellow forgives him, whether for verbal wrong or monetary wrong:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:20: The third part: On repentance for transgressions between man and the Omnipresent:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:21: There is no transgression at all, even denying the fundamental principle, that stands in the way of repentance, even if he repents at the very hour of his death.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:22: And there are four categories of atonement. If one transgressed light positive commandments and repented, he is forgiven on the spot, without moving from there. If one transgressed light negative commandments, repentance and Yom Kippur atone. If one transgressed the grave ones — those liable to karet and death at the hand of Heaven, whether positive or negative commandments, and those liable to death by the court, aside from the desecration of the Name — repentance, Yom Kippur, and suffering atone. If one transgressed the desecration of the Name, or the gravest of all, such as the class of transgressors of Israel in body, and all who go down to Gehinnom and never come up, and all who do not arise in the resurrection of the dead, and all who have no share in the World to Come, as mentioned above at length in the two parts previously discussed — repentance, Yom Kippur, suffering, and death atone:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:23: The sufferings that atone are every kind of suffering, and to what extent does this reach? Even if his garment turned inside out and he must trouble himself to turn it right side out again in order to put it on, or if he put his hand into his pocket to take out two coins and only one came up, and he has to put his hand in a second time:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:24: Repentance is such as when the very same transgression he sinned with comes his way again, and he does not do it, once and twice — such as with the same woman, at the same time and season, in similar circumstances, and in that same original place, and the like; and if he repented out of love, or even out of fear of punishment, the sin is uprooted from its root as though it had never been; but if he repented because sufferings came upon him, the sin is not fully healed and he is called one who has a blemish:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:25: Repentance requires verbal confession, and the essence of the confession is "I have sinned, I have committed iniquity, I have transgressed," but not "we have sinned, we and our fathers," and so on. And in our own Gemara (Yoma 87b) and in the Yerushalmi (end of Yoma), there is a formula for confession, and I shall abridge it and add some words to it.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 2 8:26: "Master of the world, I have committed iniquity, I have transgressed, and I have done what is evil in Your eyes, and I have stood in an evil mindset, and I have walked in a distant path, and I am now regretful of them, and would that I had not done them, and what I have done I shall not do again. May it be Your will, O Lord my God and God of my fathers, that You forgive me all my transgressions and pardon me all my iniquities and grant me atonement for all my sins that I have sinned, and committed iniquity, and transgressed before You, from the day the world was created until this very day — whether in this reincarnation or in other reincarnations, whether in prohibitions of the Torah or in prohibitions of the words of the Sages, their enactments and their safeguards and their customs — for You are the One who desires repentance. May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before You, O Lord, my Rock and my Redeemer.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 3 1:1-5: On the conduct for attaining the Holy Spirit:
The First Gate: on the nature of the worlds, in the utmost brevity, insofar as needed to understand the nature of prophecy:

Behold, the supernal Emanator, who emanated all the worlds, is called Ein Sof (the Infinite), and there is no image whatsoever within Him, neither in a name nor in a letter, nor even in the smallest strokes of the letters at all, and therefore even mere contemplation of Him is forbidden.
